subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Social Norm Nudges
description: A short lesson to help you apply Social Norm Nudges.

hook.text: A UK tax letter added one line: nine out of ten people in your area pay on time. Late payments dropped 15%.

buildup.text: Social norm nudges use peer behavior data to shift individual action. They work without mandates or penalties.

discovery.text: Opower sent energy reports comparing household use to neighbors. High users cut consumption by 2% on average.

twist.text: Low users saw they were below average and sometimes increased usage. A smiley face for low use fixed the boomerang.

climax.text: Social norm nudges are cheap and scalable. But designing them right requires testing for unintended backfire effects.

punchline.text: Show people the norm and most will follow it.

quiz.question: What boomerang effect occurred with Opower's energy reports?
options: High users ignored the reports entirely
Low users saw they were below average and increased usage

details.summary: Social norm nudges use information about what others do to shift behavior without restricting choice. Telling hotel guests that most previous guests reused towels, or telling taxpayers that most neighbors filed on time, reliably changes behavior through norm awareness.
details.whyItMatters: Social norm nudges are among the most cost-effective behavioral interventions available to policymakers. They require no new laws or incentives, just strategic communication about existing behavior patterns, yet they produce measurable changes.
takeaways: Reporting peer behavior reliably shifts individual actions toward the norm
Social norm nudges work across energy, tax, health, and environmental domains
They cost almost nothing to implement and produce consistent results

faq.question: What is the most famous social norm nudge?
faq.answer: Opower's home energy reports tell households how their energy use compares to neighbors. This simple social comparison reduces energy consumption by 2 to 4 percent on average, saving billions of kilowatt-hours across millions of households.

faq.question: Can social norm nudges backfire?
faq.answer: Yes. People who are already below the norm may increase their behavior toward it, a boomerang effect. Adding injunctive cues like smiley faces for low users prevents this by signaling approval of their current behavior.
